tldr: DINOcular is a self-supervised representation learning framework that integrates RGB images and depth to simultaneously learn visual features and 3D geometric information. By combining 3D RoPE position encodings with multi-view contrastive learning, it achieves 3D spatial awareness that outperforms prior methods of comparable scale while retaining strong semantic understanding.
hero_caption: Overall architecture of DINOcular. From input RGB-D data, it extracts lightweight local geometric features per patch (intra-patch). Meanwhile, it applies 3D RoPE (inter-patch) by incorporating depth as a third axis into the self-attention mechanism, efficiently fusing spatial structure and appearance.
overview:
Recent vision foundation models (such as DINOv2) exhibit astounding image recognition and semantic capabilities, but most are trained exclusively on monocular RGB images. In contrast, embodied systems like autonomous mobile robots, manipulators, and XR devices are equipped with explicit depth sensors such as LiDAR and stereo cameras as standard. Monocular RGB inputs alone cannot resolve physical scale ambiguity, which fundamentally limits the high-precision 3D spatial awareness required for robotics.

To address this, the authors propose "DINOcular," a self-supervised representation that takes RGB images and depth maps as input to simultaneously capture visual appearance semantics and 3D geometry. The framework introduces local geometric embeddings to capture fine surface relief inside patches in a lightweight manner, 3D RoPE to inform the self-attention mechanism of the physical spatial relationships across patches, and a multi-view self-supervised loss that encourages geometric consistency across multiple viewpoints.

In evaluation benchmarks, DINOcular significantly outperformed existing RGB-D models of comparable scale and even large RGB models on geometric tasks such as 3D correspondence prediction and object pose estimation. Furthermore, it demonstrated top-tier transfer performance on RGB-D semantic segmentation, proving that geometry and semantics can be successfully reconciled at a high level.
contributions: Proposed a transformer architecture that efficiently fuses RGB and geometric information by combining lightweight intra-patch local depth embeddings with inter-patch 3D rotary position encodings (3D RoPE).
Established a self-supervised pre-training recipe combining DINO/iBOT self-distillation with multi-view contrastive learning to acquire general visuospatial representations from RGB-D observations.

Demonstrated substantial performance gains on geometric benchmarks such as Probe3D compared to existing models of comparable scale, while simultaneously achieving exceptionally strong transfer performance on semantic segmentation.

sections.heading: Why robotic vision models need direct depth
sections.summary: While many living creatures perceive space via binocular stereopsis, current AI vision foundation models remain biased toward monocular RGB images. This work tackles learning a general-purpose model that simultaneously represents geometric structure and appearance by leveraging depth sensors found on embodied systems.
sections.details:
Across the natural world, living organisms—from primates and raptors to squid—widely possess mechanisms like binocular stereopsis to directly perceive depth. Looking at artificial systems, robots, autonomous vehicles, and XR devices are routinely equipped with stereo cameras and depth sensors, yet state-of-the-art vision foundation models are predominantly pre-trained on monocular RGB images alone. Relying solely on monocular inputs cannot avoid physical scale ambiguity, placing a hard limit on accurate 3D spatial reasoning.

A primary obstacle to incorporating depth into foundation model training has been the scarcity of depth data compared to RGB, along with significant sensor noise and missing values (heterogeneity). However, rapid recent advances in monocular and multi-view depth estimation (such as MapAnything) have made it possible to generate and complete large-scale, consistent, dense depth maps.

Most existing RGB-D fusion models are trained supervised on specific downstream tasks like segmentation, meaning they struggle to form general-purpose representations that generalize elsewhere. In this paper, the authors propose DINOcular, a framework that directly learns joint visuospatial representations from RGB-D inputs via self-supervised learning.

captions.F1: Visualization of the top 3 principal components (PCA) of extracted features. Compared to RGB-only DINO and the geometry-distilled model DUNE, DINOcular acquires features where semantics and geometric structure are cleanly integrated, particularly along monitor outlines and the 3D boundaries of home appliances.

sections.heading: Predicting 3D from RGB vs. taking depth as an input from the start
sections.summary: Vision foundation models (like DINO) and geometric prediction models (like DUSt3R) have progressed remarkably, but both take RGB as input and treat geometry as a prediction target. In contrast, this research aims for a general-purpose representation that natively fuses depth as an input modality.
sections.details:
In the lineage of vision foundation models, self-distillation approaches represented by DINO and DINOv2 capture extremely strong semantic features, but their multi-view 3D geometric consistency is known to be weak. On the other hand, approaches like DUSt3R and VGGT directly regress point clouds and 3D structures from images; however, they merely shape features aimed at predicting geometry rather than incorporating and representing depth information directly acquired from sensors.

In the context of RGB-D fusion models, dual-stream architectures combining two separate encoders were once mainstream, but research has recently shifted to token-level fusion for computational efficiency. For example, DFormerv2 injects relative distances computed from depth as an additive bias into self-attention weights. However, this merely embeds the heuristic that "nearby patches should attend more strongly to each other"; it does not embed spatial coordinates directly into the feature representations themselves.

Self-supervised methods that operate directly on point clouds, such as Sonata, also exist, but they assume large, reconstructed scene point clouds and cannot be applied directly to single-view RGB-D frames captured from a robot's camera. DINOcular sets itself apart by acquiring general-purpose representations from the most accessible format: single-view RGB-D.

sections.heading: Fusing visuospatial features with 3D RoPE and multi-view contrastive learning
sections.summary: The model adopts 3D RoPE across patches with depth as the third axis, alongside a lightweight MLP embedding within patches to capture fine surface shapes. Pre-training uses DINO/iBOT semantic distillation losses combined with a contrastive learning loss that aligns patches of the same object across different viewpoints in 3D space.
sections.details:
DINOcular's design is built on two pillars: model architecture and self-supervised training objectives.

■ Integrating Geometric Priors (Section 3.1)
To capture geometric relationships between patches (inter-patch), the authors extend Rotary Position Embedding (RoPE) into three dimensions as "3D RoPE." Alongside image plane coordinates $(u, v)$, the average patch depth $\bar{z}$ is integrated directly into the self-attention mechanism as a third rotation axis. Unlike simple distance biases, this naturally accounts for physical relative positions, including interactions between distant patches. Furthermore, to capture fine-grained surface variations and edge shapes within each patch (intra-patch), local shape features are extracted from intra-patch depth values via a lightweight linear projection layer and concatenated with the RGB patch embeddings.

■ Training Objectives (Section 3.2)
The training loss combines a semantic loss $\mathcal{L}_{sem}$ with a spatial consistency loss $\mathcal{L}_{mvi}$. The semantic loss employs DINO (global cls token distillation) and iBOT (patch-level masked reconstruction distillation). Crucially, even when RGB and local depth are masked for a patch, its depth coordinates for 3D RoPE are continuously provided.
Additionally, to pull features of patches that occupy the same physical 3D location closer together across changing viewpoints, a multi-view loss is introduced. While cosine similarity and iBOT extensions were evaluated, a ranking-based contrastive loss using SmoothAP ($\mathcal{L}_{\textrm{mv-contrastive}}$) was found to improve geometric performance most reliably.
To prevent the model from overfitting to depth and losing appearance cues, dropout is applied to the local depth embedding layer.

■ Implementation (Section 3.3)
The backbone uses a hierarchical Vision Transformer, Swin Transformer, with 3D RoPE applied across all stages.

captions.F2: The proposed multi-view pre-training workflow. Two different views of the same object are passed to the Teacher and Student networks. DINO/iBOT self-distillation losses ($L_{sem}$) are computed while pulling features of physically corresponding 3D points together via a multi-view contrastive loss ($L_{mvi}$).

sections.heading: Dominating 3D geometry benchmarks while staying competitive in segmentation
sections.summary: Trained on ImageNet and MVImgNet, the model was evaluated on both semantic understanding (RGB-D segmentation) and 3D geometric awareness (correspondence prediction and pose estimation). It outperformed comparable-scale baselines in both geometric and semantic metrics.
sections.details:
■ Training Data and Baselines (Sections 4.1–4.2)
Pre-training utilized ImageNet-1k (approx. 1.3M images) and MVImgNet2.0 (approx. 307k images across ~8 views each). Depth maps were generated with MapAnything, and object masks were extracted with SAM3. Baselines included the supervised RGB-D model DFormerv2, monocular RGB models DINO/DINOv2/DINOv3, and the geometry-distilled model DUNE.

■ Ablation Studies (Sections 4.3–4.4)
In the architectural comparison (Table 1), simply replacing DFormerv2's attention bias with 3D RoPE substantially boosted segmentation performance (mIoU) and 3D correspondence accuracy. Experiments using surface normal vectors for local geometry caused training collapse, confirming that a simple depth MLP is optimal. Comparing loss functions (Table 2) showed that only combining the contrastive loss ($\mathcal{L}_{\textrm{mv-contrastive}}$) with the DINO loss dramatically improved 3D geometry accuracy without sacrificing semantic understanding.

■ Semantic Segmentation (Section 4.5)
Under linear probing on NYU Depth V2 and SUN RGB-D (Table 3), DINOcular-S (small) outperformed DINO ViT-B, which is three times larger. It retained clearly superior semantic representations compared to DFormerv2 and DINOv2 trained on comparable data scales.

■ 3D Geometry Tasks (Sections 4.6–4.7)
On 3D correspondence prediction with NAVI and ScanNet (Table 4), the model exhibited notable strength especially under challenging conditions with large viewpoint shifts. On ScanNet, it surpassed even DINOv3 ViT-B, which was trained on far larger datasets. In CAD-free 1-shot object pose estimation (Section 4.7), DINOcular-L exceeded all baselines and DINOv3 in recall at coarser tolerance thresholds (such as $5\text{cm}$-$5^\circ$).

sections.heading: Data scale and the tradeoff between semantics and spatial awareness
sections.summary: This section outlines the limitations and challenges of the study, including evaluations restricted to medium-sized datasets and the performance tradeoff between semantics and spatial representations when introducing multi-view losses.
sections.details:
The authors highlight three main limitations of DINOcular:

- Unexplored data scaling: The study was validated on ImageNet-scale, medium-sized datasets. Whether its advantages hold when scaling to web-scale multimodal data with billions of images remains a subject for future validation.
- Difficulties in strictly fair comparison: Training datasets for DINOv2 and DINOv3 are not publicly released, preventing exact side-by-side training comparisons on identical data sources. Furthermore, DINOcular requires multi-view data, a composition that can itself impact the performance characteristics of monocular DINO-style baselines.
- Semantic vs. spatial tradeoff: As experimental results indicate, weakening the multi-view loss improves pure semantic segmentation scores, but at the expense of 3D geometric awareness. Finding the optimal balance between the two leaves room for further tuning.

sections.heading: A vital step toward true spatial understanding in robots
sections.summary: DINOcular establishes a self-supervised approach to learning visuospatial representations from RGB-D observations. This work lays the foundation for dramatically advancing spatial perception in future Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models and autonomous robots.
sections.details:
DINOcular demonstrates how explicit sensor depth can be leveraged to seamlessly unite semantic visual understanding with 3D geometric structure. Demonstrating clear advantages over prior methods of comparable scale in both semantics and geometry marks a significant advance for multimodal foundation model research.

Moving forward, scaling to larger and more diverse datasets is expected to enable direct integration into Vision-Language Models (VLMs) and Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models for robotic manipulation. It provides an exceptionally practical and insightful foundation toward robots that genuinely understand physical real-world laws and 3D spatial arrangements.

sections.heading: [Appendix] High computational efficiency and qualitative scene evaluations
sections.summary: The appendix demonstrates faster execution and lower memory usage than DFormerv2, and confirms robust performance across extreme viewpoint changes as well as indoor and outdoor segmentation through qualitative visualizations.
sections.details:
The appendix details computational efficiency and qualitative behaviors across diverse environments.

■ Computational Efficiency (Appendix B)
Compared to DFormerv2, which computes complex distance biases inside every attention operation, DINOcular runs faster and consumes less memory. It integrates 3D geometric information with only minimal latency and memory overhead relative to monocular RGB backbones.

■ Qualitative Comparisons on 3D Correspondence and Segmentation (Appendix C)
As seen in Figure F4, under challenging conditions with large camera angle changes where DINO and DUNE produce numerous incorrect matches (red lines), DINOcular densely maintains correct correspondences (green lines). In indoor scenes (Figure F6), DINOcular produces clean, sharp segmentation boundaries without the patch-boundary noise and fragmented regions observed in DFormerv2 and MultiMAE on floors and furniture. Furthermore, in outdoor driving scenes like Cityscapes (Figure F7), it demonstrates robustness in reliably recognizing roads and pedestrians without being misled by severe shadows or lighting shifts.

captions.F4: Qualitative comparison of 3D correspondence matching on the NAVI dataset. Even in difficult cases with wide viewpoint differences, DINOcular exhibits far fewer mismatches (red) than DINO or DUNE, consistently finding correct geometric correspondences (green).
captions.F6: Comparison of semantic segmentation in complex indoor scenes. While DFormerv2 and MultiMAE exhibit patchy noise and misclassifications across floor and desk surfaces, DINOcular generates uniform, high-precision masks with sharp boundaries.

takeaways: Treating depth sensors on robots as native input positional coordinates via 3D RoPE within the vision backbone—rather than merely for post-processing—is highly effective.
Combining DINO's semantic distillation loss with a multi-view contrastive loss (SmoothAP) in self-supervised learning achieves both semantic understanding and 3D geometric awareness at a high level.
Regularization techniques such as applying dropout to fine intra-patch depth embeddings are essential to prevent overfitting to spatial geometry and to acquire generalizable representations.
limitations: Pre-training datasets are limited to the ImageNet scale (hundreds of thousands to around one million images); scaling behavior on billions of images remains unverified.
Strengthening the multi-view loss improves geometric capability, but introduces a tradeoff with pure semantic segmentation performance.
Approaches using surface normal vectors as intra-patch geometric representations caused training collapse, indicating that the optimal formulation for local geometry requires further investigation.
